_readme: Story text for the screens. Writers can change any sentence. Do not change the names on the left side of the colons (the keys), or the game cannot find the text.

did_you_know._readme: "Did you know?" tips on the Build screen (PLAN.md section 6e, TASKS.md step 14): one short REAL fact per part tab, one per mission for the Instruments tab, and one (rockets) shown in the voice bar on the rocket screen. Each fact has its NASA source next to it. Only facts already checked in this project's data files are used. label = the word before the fact.
did_you_know.label: Did you know?

structure.text: MRO weighed 2,180 kg at launch, and 1,149 kg of that was fuel. Fuel is often the heaviest thing a spacecraft carries!

solar_panel.text: In a planet's shadow, solar panels make no power at all. MRO flies through Mars' shadow for about 40 minutes of every two-hour orbit.

battery.text: MRO carries a pair of rechargeable batteries to keep it running whenever it flies through the shadow of Mars.

attitude_control.text: A radio command takes 3 to 22 minutes to reach Mars. Nobody on Earth can steer a spacecraft live, so it has to point itself.

thermal_control.text: MRO uses as much as 300 watts just to run its heaters. In the shade, space is very, very cold.

antenna.text: MRO's 3-meter dish can send data home at up to about 6 megabits per second. When Mars is farthest from Earth, that drops to about 0.6.

computer.text: MRO's big camera, HiRISE, was planned to send home more than 12 terabits of pictures in its first two years. The computer stores pictures until the next radio contact with Earth.

rockets.text: NASA paid about $80 million to launch one mission on a Falcon 9, and $148 million for one on an Atlas V 401. The Falcon 9's booster lands and flies again.
rockets.source: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-launch-services-contract-for-earth-science-mission/ and https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-awards-launch-services-contract-for-lucy-mission/ (Team decision 2026-11-13: keep the real rocket numbers and teach why the Falcon 9 is cheap.)

mars.text: MRO's Context Camera weighs just 3 kg, yet it was planned to take about 3.5 terabits of pictures of Mars in its first two years.

moon.text: Apollo astronauts left seismometers on the Moon. One weighed about 11.5 kg and used only about 7 watts.

venus.text: In 1985 the Vega 1 balloon floated in the clouds of Venus. The balloon, its gondola and its helium weighed only 21.5 kg together.

air.done_voice: Fresh filter. I can breathe easy.
air.fail_text: The air filter was never swapped, so the air became unsafe to breathe.

life_food.title: Freeze-dried space food
lines: Most meals in space are freeze-dried: the water is taken out, so they are light to launch.
Astronauts add water from the ship's supply before they eat. NASA has used freeze-dried food since the Gemini missions.
life_food.source: NASA: Food on the International Space Station, https://www.nasa.gov/history/space-station-20th-food-on-iss/

life_water.title: Water is recycled
lines: Water is heavy, so space stations reuse it. Sweat, breath and even urine are cleaned back into drinking water.
The International Space Station recovers about 98% of its water.
life_water.source: NASA: NASA Achieves Water Recovery Milestone on International Space Station, https://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/iss-research/nasa-achieves-water-recovery-milestone-on-international-space-station/

life_air.title: Making air from water
lines: The space station makes oxygen by splitting water into oxygen and hydrogen with electricity from its solar panels.
Filters clean the air, and they must be swapped so the crew can keep breathing safely.
life_air.source: NASA Marshall: Environmental Control and Life Support System, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/g-657270-59-hp-environmental-control-and-life-support-system-eclss.pdf

science_calibrate.title: Keep the instruments clean
lines: Spacecraft are built in clean rooms, and their instruments are kept free of dust and germs.
That way the science is right, and Earth microbes do not travel to other worlds.

minigames._readme: Words for the three build minigames and the turn screens around them. {player} = the player's name, {score} = a score out of 100, {n} = the player number.
minigames.q_reminder: Press Q to learn why real spacecraft need this job.

assembly.title: Build job 1: Assembly
assembly.how_to: Type the name of the part being bolted on. Each finished word snaps that part onto the rocket. A wrong key freezes you for {freeze} seconds.
steps: A part name appears, like FIN or TANK.
Type its letters in order. Spaces don't count.
Finish the word and the part snaps onto the rocket behind you.
assembly.real_step: Real teams call this integration: putting every part into one spacecraft.

hammer.title: Build job 2: Hammering
hammer.how_to: Nails stick out of the rocket panel. Click a nail to hammer it in before it slides back out. Missing hits the panel and dents it.
steps: Nails pop up on the rocket panel.
Move the hammer over a nail and click to hit it.
Be quick: a nail you don't hit slides back out and stays loose.
hammer.real_step: Real teams shake-test a spacecraft so nothing falls off at launch.

fuel.title: Build job 3: Fueling
fuel.how_to: Drag the valve wheel's white knob counterclockwise and let go when the fuel gauge reaches the orange mark.
steps: An orange mark shows how far to turn the valve.
Drag the white knob around counterclockwise. The gauge fills as you turn.
Let go on the mark. The closer you are, the more points.
fuel.real_step: Real teams load propellant slowly and carefully, one of the last jobs before launch.
fuel.real_step_source: NASA CubeSat 101 (launch preparation): https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/nasa_csli_cubesat_101_508.pdf; propellant loading is one of the last steps before launch
fuel.target: Round {round} of {rounds}: turn the valve {angle}° counterclockwise

ripple._readme: The Ripple effect strip on the Build screen (PLAN.md 6c). It shows what ONE change did to the other numbers. start = the line before any change. arrow = what goes between the steps. swap = a part card change ({part} = category, {new} and {old} = card names). packed / unpacked = an instrument change. change = one number that moved. no_change = when nothing moved. now_bad = a row that just turned red ({rocket} = the rocket's name), followed by its tip. now_ok = a row that just came back inside its limit.
ripple.start: Change a card to see what else changes.

tips.budget: pick cheaper parts or a cheaper rocket
tips.mass: pick a bigger rocket or lighter parts
tips.power: pick a bigger solar panel or parts that use less power
tips.communications: pick a bigger antenna or better pointing
tips.data: pack more instruments or pick a better computer
tips.mission_lifetime: pick a stronger frame, a bigger battery or better heat control

cause_chain._readme: The cause chain on the Mission Report's finding cards (debrief, 2026-11-14), e.g. "Heavy Large frame (+120 kg) → more mass (4100 kg) → bigger rocket (Atlas V 541, 243 million $) → budget gone (712 of 671 million $)". GameState.get_cause_chain() picks the choice that pushed the resource furthest from its best option. label = the heading. arrow = between the steps. first = the first step per resource ({item} = the choice, {amount} {unit} = how much worse it is than the best option). orbit_item / window_item = how the orbit fuel and the launch date are named. more_mass and bigger_rocket = the middle steps when a heavy design forced a pricier rocket. last = the final step per resource ({value} = the total, {limit} = the limit, {rocket} = the rocket's name).
cause_chain.label: How it happened

parts._readme: The Build screen tabs and cards. tab = the short word on the tab button. name = the category's full name. hint = one line under the tabs that says what the category does. versions = one card each: name and a one-sentence description. The left-side names must match data/game_data.json ("parts").

structure.name: Structure (frame)
structure.hint: The frame holds every part together. A bigger frame is stronger and lasts longer, but it is heavier.

small.name: Small frame
small.description: Light and cheap. Just enough to hold everything.

medium.name: Medium frame
medium.description: Stronger, so the spacecraft lasts a bit longer.

large.name: Large frame
large.description: The toughest frame. Lasts the longest, weighs the most.

solar_panel.name: Solar panel
solar_panel.hint: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. Every other part needs power.

small.name: Small
small.description: Cheap and light, but makes the least power.

medium.name: Medium
medium.description: A middle choice for power, cost and weight.

large.name: Large
large.description: Lots of spare power, but heavy and costly.

battery.name: Battery
battery.hint: The battery stores power for when the spacecraft is in shadow and the sun can't reach the panels.

small.name: Small battery
small.description: Light, but it wears out sooner.

medium.name: Medium battery
medium.description: Holds more, so the mission can last longer.

large.name: Large battery
large.description: Holds the most and lasts the longest. Heavy.

attitude_control.name: Attitude control (pointing)
attitude_control.hint: Pointing keeps the spacecraft facing the right way: panels to the Sun, antenna to Earth, instruments to the target.

simple.name: Small thrusters
simple.description: Little puffs of gas turn the spacecraft. Cheap, but not very exact.

better.name: Spinning wheels
better.description: Spinning wheels turn it smoothly. Aims better, uses more power.

best.name: Wheels + star tracker
best.description: A camera finds the stars to know exactly where it points.

thermal_control.name: Thermal control (heat)
thermal_control.hint: Space is freezing in the shade and boiling in the Sun. Heat control keeps the parts at a safe temperature.

heaters.name: Heaters only
heaters.description: Electric heaters keep things warm. Simple, but they use a lot of power.

louvers.name: Heaters + louvers
louvers.description: Little shutters open and close to let heat out, so the heaters work less.

radiators.name: Radiators + heat pipes
radiators.description: Moves heat around the spacecraft on its own. Uses the least power.

antenna.name: Radio antenna
antenna.hint: The antenna sends your data home to Earth. A bigger dish sends faster, but it is heavier.

small.name: Small
small.description: Light and cheap, but too slow when Mars is far.

medium.name: Medium
medium.description: A middle size dish, a middle speed.

computer.name: Computer
computer.hint: The computer runs the spacecraft and packs the science data so more of it fits.

better.name: Better computer
better.description: Squeezes more science into the same data.

best.name: Best computer
best.description: The fastest. Squeezes the most, and is built to last.

camera_basic.name: Basic camera

laser_reflector.name: Laser reflector

scientist.description: You know spacecraft, orbits and Mars better than anyone in the room. The general just needs you to decide.

staff_card.knows: Knows the real terms. Has helped on missions.
staff_card.help: Clear hints, every time you ask.

destinations._readme: The three mission cards on the Choose a mission screen. goal = the short line under the name. goals = one sentence for each checklist id in data/destinations.json. mission_card = the Mission Room wall card (UPGRADE_PLAN_V3 B2): where, job, why, nasa; under 40 words; the longer story is behind Q on the globe.
destinations.mission_card_source: Distances: NASA fact sheets. Moon mean distance 384,400 km: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html; Mars 54.6 to 401.3 million km from Earth: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html; Venus 38.2 to 261.0 million km: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/venusfact.html (Science & Data Lead: please confirm these three lines). Trip times: destinations.json trip_days (Apollo 8 about 3 days, MRO 210 days, Pioneer Venus 198 days). NASA lines: destinations.json twins sources (Apollo seismometers until 1977, Phoenix ice 2008, MRO SHARAD buried ice, Magellan radar map) and NASA Venus facts (surface hot enough to melt lead).

moon.name: The Moon
moon.description: Land, set up seismometers far apart, and listen for moonquakes. The long lunar night has no sunlight at all.

mission_card.where: 384,400 km away. About 3 days by spacecraft.
mission_card.job: Set up seismometers and listen for moonquakes.
mission_card.why: Quakes show what the Moon is made of inside.
mission_card.nasa: Apollo astronauts left seismometers that worked until 1977.

goals.send_quake_data: Send quake data through one lunar night

mars.name: Mars
mars.description: Land, drill into the soil, and study the ice under it. Future astronauts will need that water.

mission_card.where: 55 to 401 million km away. About 7 months.
mission_card.job: Land, drill and study the ice under the soil.
mission_card.why: Future astronauts could use that ice for water.
mission_card.nasa: Phoenix dug up ice in 2008. MRO's radar finds buried ice.

goals.send_data: Send all 3 ice samples' data home

venus.name: Venus
venus.description: Nobody lands here: the surface is hot enough to melt lead, and the air would crush a lander. We study it from orbit.

mission_card.where: 38 to 261 million km away. About 6½ months.
mission_card.job: Study the storms from orbit and drop a cloud balloon.
mission_card.why: A runaway greenhouse made it the hottest planet.
mission_card.nasa: Magellan mapped it by radar. Nobody lands: the ground would melt lead.

small.name: Falcon 9
small.description: The cheapest: its booster lands and flies again. Most launch moments, tight timing.

mars_ice.name: Map the ice on Mars
mars_ice.description: Send a spacecraft to orbit Mars and take pictures to find where the ice is. Future astronauts will need that water.

solar_flare.good: Solar flare! The {computer} is protected against radiation. No harm done.
solar_flare.saved: Solar flare! The simple computer reset, but the careful assembly kept the data safe.
solar_flare.bad: Solar flare! The simple computer has no radiation protection. It reset: {days} day(s) of data lost.
solar_flare.alert: Solar flare coming! The simple computer has no radiation protection. Sound the flare alarm on the Bridge so the crew can shut it down safely.
solar_flare.fixed: Solar flare! You sounded the alarm in time: the crew shut the simple computer down safely and no data was lost.

far_from_earth.good: Halfway there. The signal to Earth is strong enough: {comms} Mb/s.
far_from_earth.bad: Radio too weak for this distance ({comms} Mb/s, needs at least {limit}). Data rate cut to {percent}%.
far_from_earth.alert: The signal is fading: our radio is too weak for this distance ({comms} Mb/s, needs at least {limit}). Re-aim the dish in the Comms Room.
far_from_earth.fixed: You re-aimed the dish exactly at Earth in time. The weak radio still gets the data home.

dust_on_panels.good: Dust on the solar panels. There is spare power ({spare} W), so everything keeps running.
dust_on_panels.saved: Dust on the solar panels. Power is short, but the well-built panels still give enough.
dust_on_panels.bad: Dust on the solar panels. Only {spare} W spare, not enough: the {instrument} is switched off.
dust_on_panels.bad_none: Dust on the solar panels. Only {spare} W spare: everything slows down. Data rate cut to {percent}%.
dust_on_panels.alert: Dust on the solar panels! Only {spare} W spare. Turn the panels to face the Sun in the Power Room before the battery runs low.
dust_on_panels.fixed: You turned the dusty panels straight at the Sun in time. Every instrument stays on.

arrival_burn.good: Arrival burn: {fuel}% fuel left, enough for a smooth arrival.
arrival_burn.bad: Arrival burn: only {fuel}% fuel left, not enough. A rough arrival: the mission loses {months} months of lifetime.
arrival_burn.alert: Only {fuel}% fuel left for the arrival. Fly a careful course-correction burn on the Bridge to save fuel.
arrival_burn.fixed: Your careful course-correction burn saved enough fuel for a smooth arrival.

heat_near_sun.good: Closer to the Sun, it gets hot. Our {thermal} get rid of the extra heat.
heat_near_sun.bad: Closer to the Sun, it gets hot. Heaters can't cool anything down: the {instrument} overheats and is switched off.
heat_near_sun.bad_none: Closer to the Sun, it gets hot. Heaters can't cool anything down: everything slows down. Data rate cut to {percent}%.
heat_near_sun.alert: Closer to the Sun, it gets hot, and heaters can't cool anything down. Reset the hot breaker in the Power Room to shut off what is overheating.
heat_near_sun.fixed: You reset the hot breaker in time. Nothing overheated.

lunar_night.good: Lunar night: no sunlight for about two Earth weeks. Our {battery} and {thermal} keep everything warm.

moon.title: No air, no parachute
moon.text: The Moon has no air to slow a lander down, so its rocket engine has to brake all the way to the ground.
moon.source: NASA: "The lack of atmosphere on the moon prevents the use of parachutes or aerobrakes to slow the descent": https://www.nasa.gov/stem-content/lunar-base-supply-egg-drop/

mars.title: Parachute, then rockets
mars.text: Mars has thin air. The Phoenix lander used a parachute first, then rocket engines for the last part down.
mars.source: NASA JPL Phoenix landing press kit (parachute at about 12.6 km, then pulsed descent thrusters to touchdown): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/phoenix-landing.pdf

venus.title: Slowing into orbit
venus.text: Nobody lands on Venus. The ship fires its engine against its motion to slow down, so Venus's gravity can hold it in orbit.
venus.source: NASA MAVEN orbit insertion: an engine burn "to slow the spacecraft so that it can be captured into Martian orbit": https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/mavens-mars-orbit-insertion/

drill.title: How the ice drill works
lines: 1. Hold E. The needle fills the bar.
2. Let go when the needle is in the GREEN zone. Too early or too late, and you try again.
3. Then RUN to the analyzer! Mars air is so thin that the ice turns straight into gas. The longer you take, the less ice is left to study.
drill.source: Real Mars ice did this: in 2008, bits of ice dug up by NASA's Phoenix lander vanished in about four days. jpl.nasa.gov/news/bright-chunks-at-phoenix-landers-mars-site-must-have-been-ice

launch3d.debris_text: Space junk ahead! Wait for it to pass, or release the spacecraft now?

liftoff.title: Liftoff!
liftoff.text: The engines push hot gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up. That is Newton's third law: every push has an equal push back.

max_pressure.title: Max Q
max_pressure.text: About a minute after liftoff, the air presses hardest on the rocket. Throttling down for a moment keeps it from being damaged.

stage_separation.title: Staging
stage_separation.text: The empty first stage drops away. With less weight to carry, the second stage can go much faster.

fairing_release.title: Fairing release
fairing_release.text: High above most of the air, the nose cone is not needed any more. It splits open and falls away to save weight.

orbit.title: Orbit
orbit.text: In orbit you are falling around Earth all the time: you move sideways so fast that you keep missing the ground.

burn.title: Leaving Earth
burn.text: One more burn speeds the spacecraft up enough to escape Earth's pull and head for {planet}.

detumble.title: Detumble
detumble.text: After separation the spacecraft can spin. Wheels inside it stop the spin so the antenna can point at Earth.

launch3d.source: liftoff (Newton's third law): https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/rocket/TRCRocket/rocket_principles.html; Max Q: https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/commercialcrew/2026/10/01/rocket-reaches-max-q-5/ and the SLS throttle-down: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/sls-5558-artemis-ii-sls-reference-guide-final-review-508-012026.pdf; staging: https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/k-12/rocket/TRCRocket/balloon_staging.html; fairing (protects the satellite from aerodynamic pressure and heating, then jettisoned): https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/pace/2024/02/01/pace-spacecraft-encapsulated-in-payload-fairing/; orbit (continuous free fall): https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/chapter3-4/; detumble (reaction wheels point the spacecraft): https://science.nasa.gov/learn/basics-of-space-flight/chapter11-2/

The rocket that carries the spacecraft from the ground into space.
The curved path a spacecraft follows around a planet or moon.
How high above the surface a spacecraft circles.

How fast data can be sent home, measured in megabits per second.
The system that turns and points the spacecraft the right way.
How long the spacecraft is built to keep working.
A choice where you gain one thing and give up another.

moon.why: We go to the Moon to hear it [b]shake[/b]. Moonquakes show what is deep inside, like an X-ray.
moon.tradeoff: The lunar night lasts two weeks with no sun. A bigger [b]battery[/b] keeps you alive, but adds mass and cost.
moon.real: Apollo astronauts left [b]seismometers[/b] on the Moon. They heard moonquakes until 1977.

mars.why: We go to Mars to find water [b]ice[/b]. Future astronauts could drink it, breathe it and make rocket fuel.
mars.tradeoff: The ice drill is heavy and power-hungry. Every kilogram of [b]mass[/b] must still fit on your rocket.
mars.real: MRO mapped Mars from orbit. The [b]Phoenix[/b] lander dug up real water ice in 2008.
mars.crew_note: No astronaut has been to Mars yet. Our crew there is a game-design choice.

venus.why: We go to Venus to chase its [b]storms[/b]. Learning why it got so hot helps us understand Earth's climate.
venus.tradeoff: The balloon and the cloud camera need [b]power[/b] and money, and the radio must be strong enough to send it home.
venus.real: Two VEGA balloons floated in Venus's clouds in 1985. NASA's [b]Magellan[/b] mapped Venus with radar.
venus.crew_note: No astronaut has been to Venus. Our crew ship there is a game-design choice.

moon.general: Listen up. We are going to the Moon to hear it shake.
moon.purpose: Find out what is inside the Moon by listening to moonquakes.
moon.why: Quakes travel through different rock in different ways. A network of seismometers works like an X-ray of the Moon's insides.
moon.tradeoff: The lunar night lasts about two Earth weeks with no sunlight. A bigger battery keeps the instruments alive, but it is heavy and costs money.
moon.based_on: Apollo astronauts left seismometers on the Moon. They recorded moonquakes until 1977.

mars.general: Listen up. We are going to Mars to find water ice.
mars.purpose: Find water ice under the ground on Mars and send the data home.
mars.why: Ice could give future astronauts water, air and rocket fuel. It also tells us how the climate of Mars changed.
mars.tradeoff: The ice drill is heavy and uses a lot of power. Every kilogram you add must still fit on the rocket.
mars.based_on: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (launched 2005) mapped Mars from orbit. The Phoenix lander (2008) dug up real water ice.

venus.general: Listen up. We are going to Venus to chase its storms.
venus.purpose: Study the fast storms in the thick clouds of Venus, from orbit and with a balloon.
venus.why: Venus is almost as big as Earth, but a runaway greenhouse effect made it the hottest planet. Learning why helps us understand our own climate.
venus.tradeoff: The balloon and the cloud camera both need power and money, and the radio must be strong enough to send it all home.
venus.based_on: The Soviet VEGA balloons floated in the clouds of Venus in 1985. NASA's Magellan mapped Venus with radar.

briefing.source: moon (Apollo seismometers until 1977, moonquakes show the inside): https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/experiment/display.action?id=1971-063C-01 and https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/missions/farside-seismic-suite/; lunar night 14 Earth days: https://science.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/lrolitho7temperaturevariation27may2014.pdf; mars (ice for drinking water, air and rocket fuel): https://www.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/mars/nasa-is-locating-ice-on-mars-with-this-new-map/; MRO launched 2005: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=2005-029A; Phoenix found water ice: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/nasa-phoenix-mars-lander-confirms-frozen-water/; venus (runaway greenhouse, hottest planet): https://science.nasa.gov/venus/venus-facts/; VEGA balloons 1985: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1984-125F; Magellan radar map: https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/magellan.html

launch_window.title: Pick a launch date

descriptions.best: The farthest date away. Waiting costs money, but Earth and the target line up just right: the shortest trip, the least fuel, and almost never a scrub. The window is short, so the launch moments are tighter.
descriptions.ok: A date a bit later. A little waiting money, a normal trip, and the weather may scrub the launch once or twice.
descriptions.poor: The soonest date: no waiting money. But the planets are badly placed: a longer trip, extra fuel, and the launch is often scrubbed again and again.

launch_window.scrub_again_poor: Scrubbed AGAIN. That is what a poor date costs.
launch_window.scrub_again: Scrubbed again. The weather will not let us go yet.
launch_window.did_you_know: Earth and Mars line up for a good launch only about every {months} months. Miss it and you wait two years!
launch_window.did_you_know_moon: Moon rockets can only leave about one week in every four, when the Moon is in the right spot. NASA's Artemis II had exactly that pattern.

weather.waited_log: Weather scrubs kept us on the pad. Waiting cost {cost} million $.

moments.title: Real Mission Moment:
moments.solar_flare: In 2003 huge solar storms hit spacecraft all over the solar system, and one science instrument on Mars Odyssey stopped working.
moments.far_from_earth: Voyager 1 is so far away that its radio signal takes almost a whole day to reach Earth.
moments.dust_on_panels: Dust on its solar panels ended NASA's InSight lander on Mars in 2022.
moments.arrival_burn: In 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter was lost at arrival because one team used pounds and another used metric units.
moments.heat_near_sun: Parker Solar Probe hides behind a heat shield that gets almost 1,400 degrees Celsius hot, while the instruments behind it stay cool.
moments.lunar_night: A night on the Moon lasts about 14 Earth days, so landers need heaters and batteries to survive it.
moments.water_leak: In 2013 water leaked into an astronaut's helmet during a spacewalk outside the space station.
moments.air_filter: On Apollo 13 the crew built an air filter out of a box, tape and plastic bags to stay alive.
moments.breaker_trip: Apollo 12 was hit by lightning twice during launch. One switch flip, SCE to AUX, brought its data back.

rooms.comms_room: The Comms Room. The big dish sends our data home to Earth.
rooms.life_support: Life Support. Food, water and air for everyone on board.

clean.title: Clean Room
clean.how_to: Hold the mouse button and wipe the dust specks off the instrument before time runs out.
steps: Dust specks land on the instrument.
Hold the mouse button and move over them to wipe them off.
Wipe as many as you can before the timer ends.
clean.real_step: Real teams call this Planetary Protection: spacecraft are built in clean rooms so Earth germs don't travel to Mars. On a crewed ship, keeping dust and germs off the gear goes on all trip long.
clean.flight_task: Wipe the dust off the instruments
clean.flight_goal: Halfway there! Go to Instruments in the Science Bay and clean them
clean.flight_log: Halfway there. Dust is floating onto the instruments in the Science Bay.
clean.flight_missed: Nobody cleaned the instruments on the way. CLEANLINESS: {score}.
